﻿                            IN THE CIRCUIT COURT FOR 
                        MONTGOMERY COUNTY, MARYLAND 
 
 *  
In the Matter of the  * Case Number C-15-CV-26-000381 
JANE CASEY HUGHES REVOCABLE * 
TRUST * 

              **************************************************************************** 
                                    OPPOSITION TO  
    RESPONDENT JOHN-MICHAEL KUCZYNSKI’S MOTION FOR INTEREST ON 
WRONGFULLY WITHHELD MANDATORY DISTRIBUTION AND FOR ORDER OF 
      IMMEDIATE PARTIAL DISTRIBUTION PENDING FINAL RESOLUTION 
 
  Comes Now, Carolina Reid, as Trustee of the Jane Casey Hughes Revocable Trust and 

files this Opposition to Respondent John-Michael Kuczynski’s (“Dr. Kuczynski”) Motion for 

Interest on Wrongfully Withheld Mandatory Distribution and for Order of Immediate Partial 

Distribution Pending Final Resolution, and states in support.  

  Dr. Kuczynski’s Motion ignores the process of Trust administration and the reality of the 

current circumstances, arising in large part from his own conduct.  

    I. THE TRUST IS NOT IN A POSITION WHERE FINAL DISTRIBUTION 
            CAN BE MADE, AND THERE IS NO OBLIGATION IMPOSED UPON 
            THE TRUSTEE TO MAKE INTERIM DISTRIBUTIONS.  
 
 First, Dr. Kuczynski demands that he receive “statutory or actual interest on the mandatory 

distribution wrongfully withheld from Plaintiff since February 1, 2025 — the date of Jane Casey 

Hughes's death and the date on which the Trust's mandatory distribution obligation was triggered.”  

There are no legal grounds under Maryland law or under the terms of the Trust for such a novel 

proposition.  

            1.  The Administration in this matter has been proper and followed a 
                necessary course. 
  
    Dr. Kuczynski’s position is faulty for at least two reasons.  First, the Trustee does not have 

an obligation to make an immediate distribution of any assets upon the death of the grantor.   The Trustee has an obligation to shepherd the administration of the Trust towards its final distribution.  

However, that final distribution cannot occur until a number of predicate actions have been taken.  

Dr. Kuczynski is a residuary beneficiary of the Trust, meaning that his ultimate share of the Trust 

is contingent upon the solvency of the Trust to pay his bequest after the payment of taxes, debts of 

the decedent, expenses for the administration of the Trust, and the distribution of any specific 

bequest.  To the extent that the Trust is solvent after all such payments are made, then Dr. 

Kuczynski’s one-third share of the remaining residuary of the Trust can be distributed.  

      The primary responsibility of the Trustee after the death of a grantor is to ensure that all 

debts of the decedent and proper tax returns have been filed and paid.  The Trustee is responsible 

for the filing of both the estate tax return and state and federal income returns.  Jane Casey Hughes 

died on February 1, 2025, before her 2024 income tax returns were due to be filed.  The Trustee is 

therefore responsible for filing Ms. Hughes’ 2024 income tax returns, short year returns for the 

period from January 1, 2025 through Ms. Hughes’ death on February 1, 2025, and income tax 

returns for the Trust beginning after the date of Ms. Hughes’ death.  All expenses relating to these 

filing obligations are the responsibility of the Trust. 

    An estate tax return is required when the value of the gross estate exceeds the applicable 

estate tax exemption at the time of death.  In order to determine the estate tax liability, the Trustee 

must identify, collect and determine the date of death value for all of the assets of the trust, 

including personal property and real property.  This process can take weeks or months, depending 

on the number and the nature of the assets held.  Once that has been completed, then the trust can 

prepare and submit a tax return outlining the expected tax obligation.   

      Ms. Hughes died as a resident of the District of Columbia and the value of her gross estate 

exceeded the 2025 D.C. estate tax exemption, requiring the filing of an estate tax return. The D.C. 



                                            2 
 estate tax return is due 10-months after the death of the grantor.  However, a 6-month extension is 

granted as a matter of course with an estimated tax payment when additional time is needed to file 

the return. 

      The Trustee has the obligation to ensure that any discrepancy between the estimated tax 

and the final tax obligation is paid.  In the event that in the intervening months the Trustee has 

distributed funds to the beneficiaries and there are additional taxes that have to be paid, the Trustee 

has an obligation to seek reimbursement from the individual beneficiaries to the extent of their 

distributed share.  The beneficiaries’ refusal to refund the Trust could lead to costly litigation, 

potentially compounding the problem as the costs and fess to collect the reimbursement from the 

beneficiaries is a Trust obligation, as well.  

      These preliminary taxing steps are recognized in the Trust document itself.  See Petition 

for Assumption of Jurisdiction, at Section III.  

    A. PAY DEATH TAXES AND SATISFY CASH NEEDS. Upon my death, my 
      trustee may, in his discretion, pay (1) my debts, administration expenses, legacies, 
    and other cash requirements of my estate (hereinafter these items and payments of 
      Taxes are referred to as "Payments"), and (2) all taxes due because of my death, 
      whether with respect to property passing under this Agreement, or under my Will… 
 

In fact, a proper reading of Section III, shows the order of the Trustee’s responsibilities prior to 

the termination of the Trust:  Pay Death Taxes And Satisfy Cash Needs; Specific Bequests Of 

Tangible Personal Property; Monetary Bequests. Only after these payments and obligations have 

been satisfied does the instruction in Section V. “Residue,” come into play.  Dr. Kuczynski’s Trust 

entitlement falls in Section V and is the last obligation to be satisfied.  

    In this case, the process of handling the tax obligations has been even more complicated.  

First, as Dr. Kuczynski is well-aware, Jane Casey Hughes was previously married to Pedro Pablo 

                                  th
Kuczynski, who later became the 66 President of Peru.  While she was not married to Mr. 


                                            3 
 Kuczynski at the time of her death, as a result of his position, the banks, including UBS Financial, 

required the satisfaction of heighten security checks prior to allowing Ms. Reid to have access to 

the post-death accounts as Trustee and in releasing records relating to the Trust. Additionally, as 

addressed in the Opposition to Dr. Kuczynski’s Motion for Accounting of the Ingleside check, the 

grantor was entitled to a sizable check for the sale of her retirement community residence as a 

refund of her entrance fee.  However, that check was not due and payable from the retirement 

community until after there was a buyer for the unit, which did not occur until the fall of 2025, and 

the amount of the refund could not be determined until after the sale.  That final proceeds amount 

was needed as a part of the tax calculations.  Moreover, the Trustee was aware of an anticipated 

refund due to the estate for the decedent’s 2024 income tax returns, but the returns had not yet 

been filed at the time the estate tax return was due. Finally, despite the Trustee’s best efforts, 

appraisals of all of the decedent’s personal property items have not yet been completed, as some 

of that property was taken by beneficiaries prior to the valuations occurring and stored in various 

locations, further delaying the ability of the Trust to finalize the accounting of the Trust value.  

      The DC estate tax extension was filed prior to December 1, 2025 and an estimated tax 

payment of nearly half a million dollars was made.  The return is now due to be filed by June 1, 

2026. 

    Dr. Kuczynski’s often cited language that the Trust is to distribute the assets “outright and 

free of trust,” does mean that distribution is required to be made immediately or within any specific 

time frame.  It requires that when the funds are distributed, they are provided outright to the 

recipients and not held in trust for the benefit of the individual.  This mundane provision regarding 

the form and recipient of the payment cannot be read to imply a time of payment or immediate 

distribution.   



                                            4 
       This is further supported by the Trust document itself, which does not contemplate 

compulsory immediate distribution.  Section VII.A. of the Trust specifically states, “The trustee 

may retain for as long as the trustee may deem proper, any of the investments or other property, 

whether real or personal, which this trust may hold at the time of my death, without regard to a 

fiduciary duty to diversify trust assets.”  See Amended Complaint, at Exhibit A, “Amended and 

Restated Trust Agreement.”  The Trust specifically contemplates post-death administration, which 

is completely inconsistent with Dr. Kuczynski’s demand.   

            2.  There is no loss to the Trust resulting from the claimed “delay.”  

    Dr. Kuczynski’s invocation of Md. Code Estates & Trusts § 14.5-1001, suggesting that this 

situation would be one in which personal liability would be imposed, is a red-herring. When the 

Trust finally distributes, Dr. Kuczynski will be entitled to his 1/3 portion of the remainder share 

of the Trust, whatever amount that may be, after all other expenses, debts, and specific legacies 

have been satisfied.  That would include whatever growth was recognized by the invested assets 

for the entirety of the period at issue.  He is not being deprived of the investment benefits of the 

funds and he will receive that at the time of the distribution.  There is no amount that would be 

owed back to the trust to make it “whole” as the trust continues to receive the benefits of its 

investments while the administration of the Trust proceeds. 

    Dr. Kuczynski also demands “the Trustee to make an immediate partial distribution to 

Plaintiff in the amount of $1,500,000.”  Again, Dr. Kuczynski’s novel demand is not based on any 

Maryland jurisprudence or any requirements of the trust agreement itself.  For the reasons stated 

above, that demand is not proper, particularly as there seems to be no end to his litigation filings 

as discussed below.  The inability for the Trustee to get the Trust to a position of final distribution 

is now largely a result of Dr. Kuczynski’s own actions. 



                                            5 
             3.  Dr. Kuczynski’s decisions to pursue wide-ranging litigation will ultimately 
                delay the distribution  of the Trust, as his claims seek varied relief 
                impacting the Trust and must be adjudicated prior to distribution, and the 
                Trust is entitled to pay for counsel’s fees from the Trust funds.  
  
      However, Dr. Kuczynski’s hyper-aggressive litigation strategy started well before any of 

the issues of the administration of the Trust could be resolved. 

            i. The first Maryland litigation is filed mere months after the death of the 
                    Grantor. 
 
    On April 17, 2025, two months after the Grantor’s death, Dr. Kuczynski filed his first 

Complaint in the Matter of John-Michael Kuczynski v. Carolina Reid, Case Number C-15-CV-25-

001897.   The details of that proceeding have been recounted in the Petition for Assumption of 

Jurisdiction and will not be restated here.  However, contrary to Dr. Kuczynski’s often repeated 

challenge that the Trustee did not have the authority to pay counsel for defending her as the Trustee 

in that matter, the Trust specifically provides for such authority, without approval from the court 

or from the beneficiaries.  Even if Dr. Kuczynski’s argument that such payment was not proper in 

the event of a finding of a breach of duty, that does not apply because that matter was settled 

through a Settlement Agreement without any findings of a breach. Therefore, there are no breach 

of duty grounds that can be used to suggest that the Trustee could not properly charge the Trust 

for the retention of professionals to defend the Trust.    

    Dr. Kuczynski now seeks to vacate the dismissal and the Settlement Agreement on the 

grounds that his attorney misrepresented the effect of the Settlement Agreement to him.  Setting 

aside the lack of substantial justification for vacating such a Settlement Agreement with the Trust 

on this basis, it will now result in additional costs to the Trust to defend the sanctity of the 

Settlement Agreement.  

 



                                            6 
             ii. Dr. Kuczynski continues his crusade in the District of Columbia Superior 
                    Court, Probate Division, in the Estate proceeding.  
 
      However, that was not the only litigation instituted by Dr. Kuczynski, as he also filed 

numerous motions in the District of Columbia’s Superior Court, Probate Division, in the 

administrative proceeding of the Estate of Jane Case Hughes.  Before the DC Court became aware 

of the litany of motions, Dr. Kuczynski had filed 23 submissions ranging from claims for 

accounting and distributions to sanctions motions against individual Trustee counsel for perceived 

misrepresentations. As it was unclear how the DC Court was going to view the question of 

jurisdiction, the Trust again, was required to spend time and resources to defend against the 

multiplicity of filings.  After filing his DC action, Dr. Kucyznski then unilaterally presented his 

filing to UBS Financial in order to have the Trust’s accounts frozen, which has prevented the 

Trustee from continuing many of the additional steps needed to come to final distribution.  

            iii. Dr. Kuczynski’s filings in this matter demonstrate an intent to continue the 
                    unrelenting attacks.  
 
      Even after the Trustee filed the present Petition for Assumption of Jurisdiction, in an effort 

to mitigate Dr. Kuczynski’s litigiousness and seek the Court’s oversight in the administration of 

the Trust, he has continued to file rapid-fire submissions on a wide range of topics, many of which 

are irrelevant to any aspect of the administration. Some of the requests for relief have been refiled 

multiple times in different forms, requiring different responses.  While the Trustee has attempted 

to be deliberative in deciding what submissions warrant a response, the sheer number of filings is 

staggering.  To that end, the Trustee filed a Motion for Injunctive Relief seeking a prefiling order 

that limits the filings, not the arguments, but this remains pending, and it is has not dissuaded Dr. 

Kuczynski from his continued filings.  

 



                                            7 
             iv.  Dr. Kuczynski has now filed a  wide-ranging attack in another parallel 
                    action in the United States Federal Court for the District of Maryland.  
 
    On March 18, 2026, the Trustee became aware that Dr. Kuczynski has now taken his wide-

ranging complaints to the Federal Court for the District of Maryland.  See Complaint in John-

Michael Kuczynski v. Carolina Reid, individually and as Trustee of the Jane Casey Huges 

Revocable Trust and as Personal Representative of the Estate of Jane Casey Hughes, Case No. 

8:26-CV-00910-TDC (without exhibits), attached hereto as Exhibit 1.  This Federal Complaint, 

filed on March 4, 2026, in the middle of these proceedings, continues to attack the same issues 

raised in the myriad of prior filings but seeks relief against Carolina Reid in all of her capacities, 

Trustee, Personal Representative, and Agent under the Power of Attorney.  As the Trust may be 

                                                                    1
obligated for attorneys’ fees incurred in the defense of each of these roles, distribution will again 

be delayed as this new matter proceeds through the Court.  

            v. The litigation creates extra expenses that continue to extend any potential 
                    timeline for distribution.  
 
      Each of these litigations and filings become additional costs and expenses for the Trust, 

which at this point, have no clear end in sight.  Dr. Kuczynski cannot be heard to complain that 

the Trustee is taking too long in making distribution, where he is constantly forcing the Trustee to 

defend against accusations that may impact the Trust. His demands relate to alleged impropriety 

in moving Trust funds, the sale of certain assets within the Trust, obtaining accountings, and his 

alleged right to distributions, among other claims, all of which are clearly claims against the 

Trustee in her role as Trustee. Dr. Kuczynski’s new claims that these allegations are against Ms. 

Reid personally is a fictitious division proposed to attempt to relieve himself of his role in the 

delays.   Even Dr. Kuczynski’s effort to remove the Trustee, which does not appear to actually be 


 
1
 The Power of Attorney includes an indemnification provision such that Ms. Reid may be entitled to have 
her expenses associated with the defense of any relevant actions reimbursed.  

                                            8 
 pending before this Court, will create additional expenses to the Trust to the extent that he is 

unsuccessful in removing the Trustee with the demonstration of the necessary standard of alleged 

malfeasance. 

    II. DISTRIBUTION IS NOT POSSIBLE UNTIL UBS FINANCIAL 
              UNFREEZES THE ACCOUNTS.  
 
      The sum effect of all of these various factors is that the Trustee never had a mandatory duty 

to distribute the residuary of the Trust at any time previous, and certainly not immediately upon 

the death of the Grantor. The fiduciary has an obligation to pay the expenses of the Trust, and until 

those amounts can be finally determined, there is no actual or alleged breach of duty for failing to 

distribute.  What can be said, with a fair amount of certainty, is that the Trust is continuing to incur 

extensive litigation costs arising from Dr. Kuczynski’s actions.  Attempting to reclaim any portion 

of distributed funds from the beneficiaries to pay necessary costs would be near impossible and 

would certainly result in substantial litigation.  The Trustee is well within her rights to withhold 

distributions until there can be a final distribution, with all known facts available.  

    It cannot be stressed enough, however, that no distributions, discretionary, mandatory or 

otherwise can be agreed to at this time because the accounts were frozen by Dr. Kuczynski’s 

improper interference.  There can be no distributions whatsoever until that situation is resolved.  

      III.  CONCLUSION 

      Maryland law also does not require that a trustee make final distribution of a trust in any 

specific time frame. Instead, prior to distribution, consistent with the Trustee’s fiduciary 

obligations to protect the Trust, there are necessary tasks that must be completed by the Trustee, 

such as obtaining valuations and filing tax returns. There is no legal authority that supports that a 

trustee has a fiduciary duty to issue an interim distribution, and certainly not under these 

circumstances where a beneficiary is aggressively attacking the Trustee’s administration of the 


                                            9 
 Trust, regardless of the merit of the claims.  There has never been an obligation to distribute upon 

any timeframe and therefore, there is no corollary claim for “interest” on any portion of the 

distribution. Dr. Kuczynski’s desire to be paid now does not create a legal obligation or impose a 

fiduciary obligation on the Trustee to do so, and his actions continue to change the amount that 

may eventually be distributed.       

 

Dated:  March 19, 2026     Respectfully submitted,

COMPLAINT FOR BREACH OF FIDUCIARY DUTY, CONVERSION,
CONSTRUCTIVE FRAUD, AND ACCOUNTING
JURY TRIAL DEMANDED
INTRODUCTION
1. This is an action by a trust beneficiary against a fiduciary who: (a) used a limited power
of attorney to transfer over $7 million in trust assets to her own daughter’s employer during the
Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Document 1 Filed 03/04/26 Page 1 of 23

-- 3 of 25 --

Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Documenti_ Filed 03/04/26 Page 2 of 23
weeks before the trust settlor’s death; (b) disclosed one of six trust accounts in a purportedly “full
and complete” accounting; (c) distributed nothing from a mandatory-distribution trust for over
thirteen months; (d) stated in writing that she is withholding distributions as punishment for
Plaintiff's exercise of his legal rights; (e) claimed personal ownership of trust assets, writing “this
is my money” to a co-beneficiary; (f) refused to identify the professionals she claims are causing
administrative delay; (g) selectively disclosed a $1,104,196.07 refund check to one beneficiary’s
counsel while concealing it from Plaintiff's counsel; and (h) systematically redacted account
information on trust checks to prevent identification of undisclosed accounts.
2. Defendant’s pattern of fiduciary abuse is not confined to this trust. In a parallel
proceeding in the Circuit Court for Montgomery County, Maryland (Case No. C-15-CV-24-
001588), a separate party represented by separate counsel has filed a $180,075.30 sanctions motion
against Defendant alleging the same pattern of conduct: using a Durable Financial Power of
Attorney to override her principal’s express wishes, filing a guardianship petition to have her
mother declared incompetent when her mother objected, and engaging in bad-faith litigation
without substantial justification.
3. Plaintiff brings in personam claims for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion, constructive
fraud, and an accounting. Plaintiff does not ask this Court to probate a will or directly administer
a trust. These are tort and equitable claims against Defendant personally, within the scope of
federal diversity jurisdiction as clarified by the Supreme Court in Marshall v. Marshall, 547 U.S.
293 (2006).

FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
A. The Trust and Its Mandatory Distribution Requirement
Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Document 1 Filed 03/04/26 Page 4 of 23

-- 6 of 25 --

Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Documenti- Filed 03/04/26 Page 5 of 23
10. Jane Casey Hughes (“Decedent”) created the Jane Casey Hughes Revocable Trust,
originally dated August 23, 1996, amended and restated August 5, 2010, with subsequent
amendments dated November 30, 2011, July 13, 2016, and September 26, 2022.
11. Section V of the Trust provides: “My trustee shall dispose of the remaining trust assets
to my three children, JOHN-MICHAEL, CAROLINA and ALEXANDRA, or their respective
estates if any of them do not survive me, outright and free of trust, the division of specific assets
comprising such shares to be made in the sole discretion of my Trustee.” (Emphasis added.)
12. This language is mandatory. The word “shall” imposes a non-discretionary duty to
distribute. The trustee’s sole discretion extends to the division of specific assets among shares, not
to whether distribution occurs at all.
13. Section V.B (First Amendment, November 30, 2011) provides that lifetime transfers
identified by the settlor shall be added back to the trust total and subtracted from the recipient
child’s share, reflecting the settlor’s “general intent that I benefit all of my children equally.”
14. Trust Section IX.D provides that any trustee who is also a beneficiary “shall act strictly
as a fiduciary” and “[n]o trustee shall have authority to make any distribution from the trust to
satisfy the trustee’s legal obligations (in the trustee’s individual capacity) for support or other
purposes.”
B. The Power of Attorney and the HEMS Limitation
15. On September 26, 2022, Decedent executed a Durable Financial Power of Attorney
appointing Defendant as attorney-in-fact. The POA was executed in Montgomery County,
Maryland and notarized by Aziz Bekishov, a Maryland notary public.
Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Document 1 Filed 03/04/26 Page 5 of 23

-- 7 of 25 --

Case 8:26-cv-00910-TDC Documenti- Filed 03/04/26 Page 6 of 23
16. On the same date, Decedent executed the September 26, 2022 amendment to the Trust,
naming Defendant as successor trustee and Defendant’s daughter, Violet Louise Reid, as backup
successor trustee.
17. Trust Section II.B governs the attorney-in-fact’s authority over trust assets during the
settlor’s lifetime. It provides: “If I have executed a Durable Power of Attorney ... the attorney-in-
fact ... shall have the right to exercise my power to withdraw income or principal from the trust as
set forth in Section II.”
18. The withdrawal power referenced in Section II is explicitly limited to “whatever
amounts are necessary for my health, education, support and maintenance”—the HEMS standard.
19. Trust Section II.B further provides: “Payments to a person other than me, my attorney-
in-fact or my guardian may only be made pursuant to an exercise of my power to withdraw income
or principal of this trust.” Any payment to a third party—including UBS Financial Services—
could only be made through the HEMS-limited withdrawal power.
20. The trustee powers set forth in Trust Section VII (continue investments, deal with
property, invest assets, borrow, lease, etc.) belong to the trustee. The attorney-in-fact does not
receive trustee powers. She receives only the HEMS withdrawal power.
C. The Unauthorized $7 Million Pre-Death Transfer
21. Decedent died on February 1, 2025.
22. The official UBS accounting for the Jane Casey Hughes Revocable Trust shows that as
of December 31, 2024, the UBS trust account held $0.00. During January 2025, $7,017,026.72

was deposited into the account. As of January 31, 2025, the account held $6,982,577.14 due to

23. The transfer of approximately $7 million therefore occurred during January 2025—
before Decedent’s death on February 1, 2025.
24. At the time of the transfer, Defendant was not trustee. She was attorney-in-fact. She
did not become successor trustee until Decedent’s death. No party disputes this.
25. As attorney-in-fact, Defendant’s sole authority over trust assets was the HEMS-limited
withdrawal power under Trust Section II.B. Transferring $7 million to UBS Financial Services
was not a withdrawal for health, education, support, or maintenance. It was an unauthorized bulk
transfer of the entire trust corpus.
26. Violet Louise Reid, Defendant’s daughter, is employed at UBS Financial Services.
Violet is also named as successor trustee in the Trust and as successor attorney-in-fact in the POA.
Defendant transferred the entirety of Decedent’s trust assets to the financial institution where her
own daughter works and where her daughter stands to assume fiduciary control.
27. Under Maryland Estates and Trusts Article § 17-113, an agent under a power of
attorney is prohibited from engaging in self-dealing transactions unless the power of attorney
expressly authorizes the specific transaction or a substantially similar transaction. The POA
contains no self-dealing waiver. Moving $7 million to where the agent’s own daughter works and
is positioned to control the assets is a self-dealing transaction prohibited by statute.

The HEMS violation—the $7 million Schwab-to-UBS transfer in January 2025—did not arise
from trust administration. It arose from Defendant’s exercise of a separate instrument—the
Durable Financial Power of Attorney—before she became trustee. POA claims are governed by a
separate statute (Md. Code, Est. & Trusts § 17-113) and fall outside the release’s scope.

COUNT I
BREACH OF FIDUCIARY DUTY
78. Plaintiff incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs.
79. Defendant owed Plaintiff fiduciary duties of loyalty, impartiality, prudence, and prompt
administration as (a) attorney-in-fact under the POA, and (b) successor trustee under the Trust.
See Md. Code, Est. & Trusts §§ 14.5-801, 14.5-802, 14.5-803; § 17-113.
80. Defendant breached those duties by: (a) transferring approximately $7 million in trust
assets to UBS Financial Services, where Defendant’s daughter is employed and positioned to
assume fiduciary control, without authority under the HEMS-limited withdrawal power and in
violation of the statutory self-dealing prohibition; (b) failing to distribute any trust assets to any
beneficiary for over thirteen months despite mandatory distribution language; (c) withholding

    An estate tax return is required when the value of the gross estate exceeds the applicable 

estate tax exemption at the time of death.  In order to determine the estate tax liability, the Trustee

on the number and the nature of the assets held.  Once that has been completed, then the trust can 

prepare and submit a tax return outlining the expected tax obligation.   AGAIN, MORE ABSTRACTIONS; MORE LECTURES ABOUT "A" TRUSTEE'S DUTY'S; PUFFERY; FAILURE TO ADDRESS MY SPECIFIC POINTS ABOUT THIS TRUSTEE'S FAILURES.

ARGUMENT
A.
Legal Standard
Although the “American Rule” regarding attorneys' fees is that each party
bears their own costs, MD. RULE 1·341 provides a “limited exception” intended “to
function primarily as a deterrent” against abusive litigation. Christian v. Maternal·
Fetal Medicine Assocs. of Maryland, LLC, 459 Md. 1, 18-19 (2018) (quoting, in part,
Worsham v. Greenfield, 435 Md. 349, 369 (2013)). Rule 1-341 governs award of
reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs for proceedings brought or defended in bad faith
or without substantial justification. The Rule states that:
In any civil action, if the court finds that the conduct of any
party in maintaining or defending any proceeding was in
17

bad faith or without substantial justification, the court, on
motion by an adverse party, may require the offending
party or the attorney advising the conduct or both of them
to pay to the adverse party the costs of the proceeding and
the reasonable expenses, including reasonable attorneys'
fees, incurred by the adverse party in opposing it.
Id. (emphasis added).
Rule 1·341 acts not as punishment, but rather “as a mechanism to place the
wronged party in the same position as if the offending conduct has not occurred.”
Christian 459 Md. at 19 (internal quotations
and citations omitted). Such offending
conduct includes litigation brought: (a) in bad faith, meaning “vexatiously, for the
purpose of harassment or unreasonable delay, or for other improper reasons[,]” Inlet
Assocs. v. Harrison Inn Inlet, Inc., 324 Md. 254, 268 (1991) (emphasis added); or (b)
without substantial justification, whereby the offending party lacked any “reasonable
basis for believing that the claims would generate an issue of fact for the fact finder[.]”
Id. “[C]onduct lacks substantial justification
when there is no basis in law and/or in
fact to support the plaintiff's claim against the defendants who seek fees and costs.”
Johnson v. Baker, 84 Md. App. 521, 529 (1990); see also Garcia v. Foulger Pratt Dev.,
Inc., 155 Md. App.
634, 676 (2003) (stating that “[f]or there to be substantial
justification, the litigant's position must be fairly debatable and within the realm of
legitimate advocacy.”).
For the latter example, the Court “must conduct an
examination of the merits under the totality of the circumstances presented to the
court[.]” Christian, 459 Md. at 23 (internal
quotations and citations omitted).
In order to grant a motion under Rule 1-341, the Court “must first find that
the conduct of a party during a proceeding, in defending or maintaining the action,
18

was without substantial justification or was done in bad faith. Second, the judge
must find that the acts committed in bad faith or without substantial justification
warrant the assessment of attorney’s fees.” Bennett v. Ashcraft & Gerel, LLP, No. 31,
Sept. Term, 2022, 2023 WL 5665589, at *24 (Md. Ct. Spec. App. Sept. 1, 2023)
(internal citations and quotations omitted). “A trial judge must be satisfied by a
preponderance of the evidence that a party has acted in bad faith or without
substantial justification.” Garcia, 155 Md. App.
at 677.
B.
The Preponderance Of The Evidence Establishes That The Above-
Captioned Matter Was Initiated And Maintained In Bad Faith And
Without Substantial Justification, And Justify An Award Of The
Personal Representative’s Reasonable Attorneys’ Fees And Costs.
1.
The Evidence Establishes That Mr. Hughes Had The Capacity To
Execute The Will And Was Not Subjected To Undue Influence,
Rendering Ms. Reid’s Arguments To The Contrary As Lacking
Any Substantial Justification.
a.
Mr. Hughes Had Capacity On September 26, 2022.
First, as discussed supra, Ms. Reid’s
allegations that the Will was the product
of undue influence, or that Mr. Hughes lacked capacity at the time of its execution on
September 26, 2022, lack any substantial justification. “There is a presumption that
one has the capacity to execute a valid will.” Jackson v. Jackson, 249 Md. 170, 175
(1968). The party challenging capacity bears the burden of proof. Arbogast, Exec. v.
MacMillan, 221 Md. 516, 523 (1960).
“To rebut that presumption, one challenging a
will for lack of testamentary capacity must prove either that the testator was
suffering from a permanent insanity before he made his will, and therefore would
have been insane when he made the will; or, although not permanently insane, he
was of unsound mind when he made the will.” Dougherty v. Rubenstein, 172 Md.
19

App. 269, 284 (2007) (emphasis added); see also Jackson, 249 Md. at 175 (noting that
“[e]ccentricity, old age, debility, and disappointment of reasonable expectations of
prospective beneficiaries are not the yardsticks by which mental capacity can be
measured.” (citation omitted)). The analysis turns on an examination of the testator’s
external acts and appearances at the time of making the will, and whether “at the
time of making the will” the testator
had a full understanding of the nature of the business in
which he was engaged; a recollection of the property which
he intended to dispose and the persons to whom he meant
to give it, and the relative claims of the different persons
who were or should have been the objects of his bounty.
Ritter v. Ritter, 114 Md. App. 99, 105 (1997) (citation omitted).
Mr. Hughes’ external acts and appearances, according to Ms. Webster,
establish that he had a full understanding of his assets, and his testamentary
intentions for same, when he developed his estate plan in 2022, and executed the Will
and Trust Agreement on September 26 of that year. See generally Exhibit D.
Ms.
Webster’s assessment is corroborated by a review of Mr. Hughes’ medical records,
which, according to the Personal Representative’s designated expert, reveal no
-
indications of any mental disorders or dementia (despite what Ms. Reid alleged in her
Petition). See generally Exhibit L. This assessment is further corroborated by Mr.
Hughes’ detailed 2022 Memo, in which he sets forth in granular detail, and in
relevant part, his reasoning for donating his interest in the Hamlet Place Unit to
Carleton College. See generally Exhibit Y. Indeed, even Ms. Reid expressed
contemporaneously following Mr. Hughes death that, just days before, she had a
“lovely” time at dinner with him, and expressed no concern about him being of
20

unsound mind. See generally Exhibit M. Simply put, there is no basis in
law and in
fact to support Ms. Reid’s claim that Mr. Hughes lacked capacity when he executed
his Will.
b.
Mr.
Hughes Was Not Subjected To Undue Influence On
September 26, 2022.
Similarly, the burden to establish undue influence is “a heavy one.” Zook v.
Pesce, 438 Md. 232, 249 (2013).
To be “undue” influence, it “must be exerted to such
a degree as to amount to force or coercion, destroying free agency.” Koppal v. Soules,
189 Md. 346, 351 (1947). As such, undue influence consists of “physical or moral
coercion that forces a testator to follow another’s judgment instead of his own.” Moore
v. Smith, 321 Md. 347, 353 (1990). “Mere suspicion is not enough”
to meet this
burden. Waple v. Hall, 248 Md. 642, 668 (1968); see also Carter v. Aramark Sports &
Ent. Servs., Inc., 153 Md. App. 210, 225 (2003) (“[C]onclusory statements, conjecture,
or speculation by the party resisting the motion will not defeat summary judgment[,]
and an opposing party’s facts must be material and of a substantial nature, not
fanciful,
frivolous,
gauzy,
spurious,
irrelevant,
gossamer
inferences,
conjectural, speculative, nor merely suspicions.” (internal quotations and citations
omitted)). Rather, independent evidence of improper influence being brought to bear
on the testator must be adduced. Woodruff v. Linthicum, 158 Md. 603, 610 (1930)).
Because there is no bright-line test for undue influence, the Court of Appeals
in Moore identified seven factors characteristic of
the presence of undue influence: (1)
the benefactor and beneficiary are involved in a relationship of confidence and trust;
(2) the will contains substantial benefit to the beneficiary; (3) the beneficiary causes
21

or
assists in effecting execution of the will; (4) there is an opportunity to exert
influence; (5) the will contains an unnatural disposition; (6) the bequests constitute a
change from a former will; and (7) the testator is highly susceptible to the influence
of others. Moore, 321 Md. at
353. Although a party need not prove the presence of
-
all seven factors, the first and seventh factors (relationship of confidence and trust,
and high susceptibility to undue influence) are crucial and necessary to find undue
influence. Green v. McClintock, 218 Md. App. 336, 369 (2014).
Although Ms. Webster acknowledged Mr. Hughes’ physical deterioration,
which is also corroborated by his medical records, there is no evidence that any person
holding a position of trust and confidence over Mr. Hughes abused that position
through the kind of “physical or moral coercion” that forced Mr. Hughes to follow any
judgment other than his own.
To the contrary, Ms. Webster recounts how “Mr.
Hughes always expressed his wishes firmly and clearly to me, and questioned my
recommendations closely at a level of detail that was appropriate.” See
Exhibit D at
4, ¶ 16.
But perhaps more tellingly, it was not until months after Mr. Hughes died – by
which time Ms. Reid would have learned of his inter vivos donation of
his interest in
the Hamlet Place Unit – that she suddenly raised alarm about Mr. Hughes’ debility
and supposed high susceptibility to undue influence. But in September 2022, she was
aware that Mr. and Mrs. Hughes were executing estate planning documents, and that
22

Mr. Nordholm would be assisting them – and she raised no alarm.
-
13
No one did –
because there was nothing about which to be alarmed. There is simply no evidence
of undue influence in this matter, and Ms. Reid’s allegations of such are similarly
without any basis in law and in fact.
2.
Ms. Reid Had An Improper Motive In Bringing These Allegations
Because She Wanted To Receive The Hamlet Place Herself, And She And
Her Counsel Maintained These Proceedings Even After Mrs. Hughes
Made It Known That Doing So Was Against Her Wishes.
As the proceedings in this matter progressed, the factual thrust behind Ms.
Reid’s claims crystallized, specifically that Mr. Hughes never intended to deprive Mrs.
Hughes of her ability receive his interest in the Hamlet Place Unit upon his death,
and to live there following his death. Of course, such claims are false. Mrs. Hughes
herself told Ms. Webster (who represented both Mr. and Mrs. Hughes) that she did
not want her husband’s interest in the Hamlet Place Unit.
The only person who
wanted Mr. Hughes’ interest in the Hamlet Place Unit was Ms. Reid. But since she
lacked standing to challenge the validity of Mr. Hughes’ Will directly, she did so
through her mother as the latter’s attorney-in-fact – disregarding her mother’s own
wishes.
Maryland law is clear that an attorney-in-fact shall, amongst other things,
“[a]ct in accordance with the principal’s reasonable expectations to the extent actually
known by the agent and, otherwise, act in the principal’s best interest[,] [and] [a]ct
with care, competence, and diligence for the best interest of the principal[.]” See
MD.
13 Neither, of course, did Mrs. Hughes – in whose name all of this has been alleged. Indeed,
Ms. Reid presumably cannot challenge Mrs. Hughes’ capacity during that time since doing so would
invalidate the operative POA under which she has acted this entire time.
23

ANN. CODE, EST. & TRUSTS § 17-113(a)(1)-(2). Similarly, an attorney-in-fact shall
“[a]ct loyally for the principal’s benefit[,] [and] Act so as not to create a conflict of
interest that impairs the agent’s ability to act impartially in the principal’s best
interest[.]” See MD. ANN. CODE, EST. &
TRUSTS § 17-113(b)(1)-(2). Maryland law is
clear that
[T]he main duty of an agent is loyalty to the interest of
[her] principal. Thus, in exercising granted powers under
a power of attorney, the attorney in fact is bound to act for
the benefit of his principal and must avoid where possible
that which is detrimental unless expressly authorized…
Even if a general discretion is vested in the agent, it is not
deemed to be unlimited. But it must be exercised in a
reasonable manner, and cannot be resorted to in order to
justify acts, which the principal could not be presumed to
intend, or which would defeat, and not promote, the
apparent end or purpose, for which the power was given.
[I]t is a universal principle in the law of agency, that the
powers of the agent are to be exercised for the benefit of the
principal only, and not of the agent or of third parties. A
power to do all acts that the principal could do, or all acts
of a certain description, for and in the name of the
principal, is limited to the doing of them for the use and
benefit of the principal only, as much as if it were so
expressed.
King v. Bankerd, 303 Md. 98, 108-09 (1985) (internal citations omitted) (internal
emphasis removed) (additional emphasis added).
Here, Ms. Reid acted solely out of her own self-interest, and disregarded the
intentions of Mrs. Hughes, the principal. Mrs. Hughes communicated with Mr. Stein
that she did not want this matter to proceed. And regardless whether Mrs. Hughes
had any assistance in drafting her June 1 E-mail, she clearly instructed her other
daughter, Alex, to send it to Mr. Stein. See
Exhibit P at 1. Plus, she sought assistance
from Ms. Webster to stop this matter. See generally Exhibit R. None of
these efforts
24

were successful. Instead, and perhaps most troubling, Mrs. Hughes was under the
clear impression that this matter had been dismissed, and said as much to Mr.
Nordholm. These statements suggest that Ms. Reid lied to Mrs. Hughes about the
-
actions she was taking in her name.
For these reasons, the meeting between Mrs. Hughes, Ms. Reid, and Mr. Stein
the details of which Ms. Reid has shielded under an assertion of the attorney-client
–
privilege – are of critical importance.
While the date of this meeting remains
undisclosed, the November 14 Reply explains that following this meeting, Ms. Reid
“consistent with her authority in the [POA], determined that it was in Mrs. Hughes’
best interest to proceed with the litigation and as a result, the litigation continued.”
See Reply to Mtn. for Voluntary Dismissal
at 6-7, ¶ 15 (emphasis added). But, as
discussed supra, it is inconsistent for
Ms. Reid to exercise the authority granted her
under the POA for a purpose benefitting herself as opposed to Mrs. Hughes.
Even more disconcerting, mere months after this matter was initiated, Ms.
Reid – through Mr. Stein – initiated guardianship proceedings in the District of
Columbia for Mrs. Hughes. See generally id., Exs. 12-16. As this matter progressed,
Ms. Reid’s filings increasingly stressed Mrs. Hughes’ incompetence.
Even the
affidavit that Ms. Reid provided in support of her November 14 Reply stated, in part,
that she “believed that [Mrs. Hughes’] cognitive inabilities prevented her from
making reasonable decisions with respect to her assets and that, as her Attorney-in-
Fact, it was in her best interest to pursue litigation to recover for losses [Ms. Reid]
believe[s] she sustained by [Mr. Hughes’] execution of his [Will] and the [Trust
25

Agreement].” See id., Ex. 6 at 1, ¶ 4 (emphasis
added). But, as discussed supra, no
one challenged Mrs. Hughes’ cognitive health when she executed her POA, or when
she explained to Ms. Webster that she did not want to receive any interest in the
Hamlet Place Unit.
It was only after Mrs. Hughes learned of this matter, and
expressed her desire for it to be dropped, that she suddenly became incompetent. The
improper motive behind Ms. Reid’s initiation of this matter is clear.
3.
Under The Totality Of The Circumstances Set Forth Herein, An Award
Of Reasonable Attorneys’ Fees And Costs Are Appropriate.
The totality of the circumstances set forth supra
establish not only that Ms.
Reid’s claims were brought in bad faith and without substantial justification, but that
an award of reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs are warranted.
Mr. Nordholm
therefore requests an award of attorneys’ fees and costs in the amount of
$180,075.30,14 based on a reasonable hourly rate, which was incurred in defending
this action since June 2023.15
This amount is fair and reasonable, and the
undersigned’s Verified Statement concerning the amount sought to be awarded is
attached hereto as Exhibit Z.
CONCLUSION
In his 2022 Memo, Mr. Hughes articulated a key reason why he wanted to
donate his interest in the Hamlet Place Unit prior to his death to Carleton College:
Now the issue is how to handle all this peacefully without
disturbing [Mrs. Hughes] and raising a new rumpus with
14 This amount specifically breaks down as $167,837.50 in fees, and an additional $12,237.80
in costs, through January 31, 2025.
15 Mr. Nordholm reserves the right to supplement this demand with the additional attorneys’
fees and costs associated with the preparation and filing of this Motion, and any hearing(s) related
thereto, that have yet to be invoiced.
26

[Ms. Reid]. I have intended to hold onto the [Hamlet Place
Unit] for tax reasons – avoid big capital gains if I sold now,
and instead get the benefit for my heirs of the step-up in
basis.
But this would mean my selecting my heirs and
pitch Evan or Allan into a row with [Ms. Reid]…[A] gift to
Carleton – a charity – should be non-taxable. This must be
confirmed. But Carolina would get a softer landing. She
would find it hard to argue against a college gift. If I were
to deed it to Evan or Allan, there would be a family row.
See Exhibit Y at 17-18 (emphasis added).
Mr. Hughes’ impressions were correct –
disposition of his interest of the Hamlet Place Unit to someone other than Ms. Reid
has indeed caused a “row.”
One brought in bad faith and without substantial
justification. And one in which Ms. Reid acted contrary to clear Maryland law
controlling her conduct as Mrs. Hughes’ attorney-in-fact. Rule 1-341 is designed to
address circumstances such as these, and the requested award for attorneys’ fees and
costs is reasonable and justified. This Motion should be granted.
WHEREFORE, for these reasons, the Personal Representative respectfully
requests that this Motion be GRANTED, and that: (a) the Court enter an award of
reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs – the final amount of which to be determined
following a merits hearing – in favor of the Personal Representative and against,
jointly and severally, Petitioner Carolina Reid and her counsel, Jesse Stein; and (b)
and such further relief that the Court deems appropriate under the facts and
circumstances set forth herein.

Conflicts. As you know, there are certain ethical rules that bind us as attorneys when we
represent you as a couple. As your joint attorney, we represent both of your interests and cannot
advocate the interests of one of you over the other. We also cannot receive information from
either of you that is not shared with the other. Provided you are in agreement about your estate
plan, the joint representation should not present a problem. However, if, during the course of our

representing both of you, or if either of you asks us to take sides against the other, or to have
confidential communications, we will be forced to withdraw from further joint representation,
and you may need to obtain separate counsel. By signing this letter, you confirm that you wish
to be represented jointly.

I, Thomas Lowe Hughes, presently domiciled and resident of
Montgomery County, Maryland, do make, publish, and declare
this to be my Will, hereby revoking all former Wills and
Codicils.
I am married to Jane Casey Hughes (herein referred to a JANE).
From a prior marriage to Jean Reiman Hughes (JEAN),
deceased in 1991, I have two sons: Thomas Evan Hughes
(EVAN) and Allan Cameron Hughes (ALLAN). I have no
grandchildren.
FIRST
I direct that my mortal remains be cremated at a cost to be
determined by the Personal Representatives of my estate,
notwithstanding any provision of law to the contrary. I direct
my Personal Representatives to distribute up to one-half (1/2)
of my ashes to JANE, if she survives me and if she so desires.
The remaining portion of my ashes shall be interred in my plot
in Lakewood Cemetery in Minneapolis, Minnesota,
I authorize my Personal Representatives, as soon as
practicable after my death, to pay my enforceable debts and
the expenses of my last illness, cremation, funeral and/or
memorial services, without regard to any statutory limit on
such expense and without the necessity of any court order.
SECOND
I direct that my Personal Representatives deliver to my
- nephew, Bradford Nordholm (BRAD), as soon as practicable,

the copies of my records, notes, and files relating to my.
Hohenzollern-Schaberg-Hentig family history (originals at Yale
University Library). The decision of BRAD as to which items
are part of this collection shall be conclusive and binding upon
all persons. I understand that when BRAD is finished with

England Historic and Genealogical Society in Boston
Massachusetts, to become part of their permanent manuscript
collection.
I direct that all other family history files are to be deposited
within ninety days after my death with the same above
mentioned manuscript collection at the New England Historic
and Genealogical Society in Boston.
I further direct that the remainder of my personal files
containing my diaries, correspondence, documents from the.
State Department and Carnegie Endowment, and records of my
non-cash donations of family materials to Yale University,
Carleton College, and the Minnesota Historical Society, be sent
to the Library of Congress to join the extensive Thomas Lowe
Hughes manuscript collection already on deposit there.
I direct, however, that my personal income tax returns and
medical records not be included in this bequest, but should be
discarded,
I further direct that the oil portraits in the living room, dining
room, breakfast room, and guest room should be given to the
family members who want them. I shall prepare signed and
dated lists describing them for the assistance of my Personal
Representatives

Subject to the above, I leave all the contents of my home on
Western Avenue to JANE if she survives me, with the request
that any antiques from my family be given to my sons EVAN or
ALLAN or to BRAD in JANE's discretion during her lifetime or
left to them upon her death. Provided, however, that I
expressly declare that I do not intend to create any trust with
respect to such property.
If JANE does not survive me, the contents of my Western
Avenue home should go to my sons EVAN and ALLAN, in as
nearly equal shares as practicable. If they are not able to agree
on the disposition of any item, the decision of my Personal
Representatives shall be final.
I direct that all the contents of my co-op property in Hamlet
Place should go to JANE if she survives me. If she does not
survive me, the contents of this property should go to my sons,
EVAN and ALLAN, in as nearly equal shares as practicable, If

The costs to store, insure and deliver any items of my tangible
personal property are to be paid as an expense of

Personal Representatives to discard or donate any item not
disposed of specifically above in Article SECOND,
THIRD
I direct the sale of my Western Avenue home as soon after my
death as practicable, this transaction to be completed within
one year of my death if possible. But I grant my Personal
Representatives full authority and discretion to accomplish the
sale upon the terms and conditions and within such

timeframes as they determine are in the best interest of my

Provided, however, that if JANE survives me, she is allowed
ample time to arrange for the disposition of her personal

may continue to live there free of any rental obligation. All
costs of maintaining that residence or preparing it for sale shall
be paid as expenses of administration of my estate.
Since the original purchase of the Western Avenue residence in
1967, my family has benefitted so greatly from the foresight
and ingenuity of my first wife JEAN in locating and furnishing
said residence, I desire to maximize the proceeds from the sale
of said residence to benefit both of our sons EVAN and ALLAN.
Hence the residue of my estate (including any property over
which I may have testamentary power or control) shall be
divided into equal shares: one share to each then surviving
son of mine, each such share to be distributed outright to such
son; provided further that if my son EVAN predeceases me, but
is survived by his wife, Lynn McCary Hughes (hereinafter"

I direct that my full interest in my Hamlet Place co-op go to

not survive me, it should be added to the residue of my estate.
FOURTH
In the event that I am survived by neither of my sons nor

distributed to JANE. If none of EVAN, ALLAN, LYNN or JANE
survives me, then to my heirs-at law as then determined. The

AFFIDAVIT OF AEN W. WEBSTER
I, Aen W. Webster, declare as follows:
1.
I am over the age of eighteen (18), competent to be a witness in this matter, and
have personal knowledge of the facts set forth in this affidavit.
2.
I am an attorney with the COCHRAN LAW GROUP in Tysons, VA. My practice is
focused on estate planning and administration. I received my undergraduate degree from Yale
College, and my J.D. from Stanford Law School.
3.
I am the drafting attorney for the Last Will and Testament, dated September 26,
2022, of Thomas Lowe Hughes ("Mr. Hughes") and the Thomas Lowe Hughes Revocable Trust
under agreement dated September 26, 2022. I therefore have personal knowledge of the
circumstances surrounding the preparation of this Will and trust, as well as the allegations raised
in this matter.
4.
Had I been called to testify at either deposition or trial in this matter, I would have
testified under oath as follows.
5.
I represented Mr. Hughes and his wife, Jane Casey Hughes ("Mrs. Hughes"), jointly
in estate planning attorney from 2016 through 2022.
6.
Mr. Hughes asked me to prepare a revocable trust with the dispositive provisions
of his existing Will. Mr. Hughes stated that he wished to use a revocable trust to avoid probate.
1

Mr. Hughes also told me that his nephew, Bradford Nordholm ("Mr. Nordholm"), who had long
been nominated as a fiduciary under Mr. Hughes's Will, power of attorney, and advance directive,
had recently moved to the DC area and would assist him with the mechanics of this process (i.e .,
facilitating calls, e-mails, printing drafts).
7.
After several phone conversations to confirm Mr. Hughes's wishes, at least one of
which was a conference call with both Mr. Hughes and Mr. Nordholm, I prepared drafts of a new
Will and a Revocable Trust. Mr. Hughes then reviewed these drafts, and we had at least one
subsequent call to review Mr. Hughes's questions.
8.
It was during one such call that Mr. Hughes told me that he had decided not to leave
the co-op at Hamlet Place to Mrs. Hughes (as previously had been provided in Mr. Hughes' prior
estate planning) because Mrs. Hughes wished to move to her apartment at Ingleside after his death,
and, as a result, she did not want to live at Hamlet Place (which previously had been the couple's
plan for Mrs. Hughes's residence if she survived Mr. Hughes). I told Mr. Hughes that I could not
make that change without first speaking with Mrs. Hughes because I represented the couple jointly,
and I could not have an ex parte conversation with Mr. Hughes about a matter that also affected
her interest.
9.
Sometime later, Mrs. Hughes called me while Mr. Hughes was in the room with
her, and she and I discussed the change in the disposition of the Hamlet Place co-op. Mrs. Hughes
told me that she was aware of Mr. Hughes' plan and that she had no objection to the change because
she did not want the Hamlet Place co-op.
10. I then provided a revised draft of the revocable trust for Mr. Hughes to review.
When he had no further questions and was satisfied with his draft documents, I prepared the final
2

documents for execution at Mr. Hughes's home with a mobile notary. Mr. Nordholm printed the
final documents for execution.
11.
In the meantime, I had learned that Mrs. Hughes had misplaced some original
documents that she had signed carlier that year at a bank near the Hughes home. I suggested that
Mrs. Hughes re-sign those documents with the notary and witnesses who would be present at the
house when Mr. Hughes signed his documents. Mrs. Hughes was happy with this arrangement, as
was her daughter, Carolina Reid ("Ms. Reid"), who had plans to be in Maryland around the time
of the execution. Mrs. Hughes told me that she did not want any changes to her documents and
would sign the same versions that she had signed a few months earlier. When Ms. Reid became
unable to make the trip, Mr. Nordholm agreed to assist both Mr. and Mrs. Hughes with the
execution of their respective documents, a solution to which Ms. Reid agreed. Ms. Reid was thus
aware that Mr. and Mrs. Hughes were planning to execute estate planning documents together at
the Hughes home in September 2022.
12. Upon my information and belief, Mrs. Hughes went to the church next door to get
two witnesses and brought back two of the clergy to act as such.
13. After the execution, Mr. Nordholm had both sets of documents imaged. He sent
Mrs. Hughes' original documents to me. Per my communication with Mrs. Hughes, Ms. Reid was
to come to my office to pick up those originals the next time she was in town, but that did not
occur and those originals remain in the document safe at my office.
14. It is my understanding that Mr. Nordholm retained Mr. Hughes's original
documents. Mr. Nordholm then assisted Mr. Hughes with the transfer of Mr. Hughes's
individually owned assets into the revocable trust, either by direct transfer or by registration to pay
on death or transfer on death, depending on the type of account.
3

15.
During the entire time that I represented Mr. and Mrs. Hughes, I was impressed
with his mental acuity and determination. I had no concern about Mr. Hughes' cognitive ability
at any point during my representation. He asked good, often highly detailed, questions about his
draft documents and the process of estate and trust administration. He also demonstrated a full
understanding of what he owned and the general value of his assets, expressed clear and consistent
wishes regarding the people for whom he wished to provide in his estate plan, and he expressed a
clear understanding of the process of estate planning and of the import of his desired estate plan.
While I understood that Mr. Hughes's physical health declined over the course of my
representation, and that he needed assistance with practical matters such as printing documents, I
never had any concern that his physical decline affected his cognitive ability, his ability to
communicate, or his capacity to execute any estate planning document.
16. In addition, I was never concerned about any undue influence being imposed on
Mr. Hughes by any person, or that he added provisions to his estate planning documents that were
counter to his own wishes. Mr. Hughes always expressed his wishes firmly and clearly to me, and
questioned my recommendations closely at a level of detail that was appropriate.
17. Mrs. Hughes was fully aware that Mr. Hughes was working on new estate planning
documents, and - at minimum - she was aware of the change he was making about the disposition
of his co-op at Hamlet Place because, as noted supra, she and I specifically discussed that
disposition. While I do not know whether Mrs. Hughes specifically read any of Mr. Hughes's
estate planning documents, I do know that Mr. and Mrs. Hughes assisted each other with e-mails
and printing of documents and, as a result, that Mrs. Hughes had access to her husband's draft
documents throughout the process.
4

18. I did not have any concern about Mrs. Hughes's cognitive ability during this time.
Although Ms. Reid had told me that Mrs. Hughes was increasingly physically frail, I did not
observe any change in Mrs. Hughes's ability to understand and communicate, and she was always
clear in giving me direction regarding her wishes. While her ability to use technology and keep
track of papers may have declined, I did not observe any decline in Mrs. Hughes's mental acuity
and clarity of communication. During this period of time, my communications with Mrs. Hughes
were limited to telephone and e-mail, but at some point around the time of the document execution
at the Hughes home, I briefly encountered Mrs. Hughes when I was driving through the
neighborhood and she was walking out to do an errand. She appeared strong and alert to me at that
time.
I, Aen W. Webster, solemnly affirm under the penalties of perjury and upon personal
knowledge that the contents of this affidavit are true.
Krebse

Aen W. Webster

and wherever located, belonging to me at my death and remaining after the payment of, or
appropriate provision for, debts, taxes, funeral and administration expenses and any other lawful
charges against my estate, whether provided in this Will or otherwise. My Residuary Estate shall
not include any property over which I have a power of appointment at the time of my death.

THOMAS LOWE HUGHES REVOCABLE TRUST
THIS TRUST AGREEMENT is entered into this 24 day of Septista
2022, by THOMAS LOWE HUGHES, a resident and domiciliary of the State of Maryland, as
Grantor (the "Grantor") and as Trustee (the "Trustee").
INTRODUCTION
(1) The Grantor desires to establish a revocable trust for his lifetime benefit
and also to provide for his wife, JANE CASEY HUGHES ("JANE"), and his children,
THOMAS EVAN HUGHES ("EVAN") and ALLAN CAMERON HUGHES ("ALLAN"). The
revocable trust initially created hereunder shall be known as the THOMAS LOWE HUGHES
REVOCABLE TRUST.
(2) The Trustee agrees to hold, manage, and administer the property initially
contributed hereunder, and any additions, together with the proceeds and reinvestments thereof,
in trust, for the purposes and upon the terms and conditions set forth in this Agreement.
1.
Administration During Grantor's Lifetime. During the Grantor's lifetime,
the Trustee shall pay to or apply for the benefit of the Grantor or others so much or all of the net
income and principal of the trust as the Grantor, without limit, may direct. However, for any
periods during which the Grantor is incapacitated, as hereinafter defined, the Trustee shall pay to
or apply for the benefit of the Grantor so much or all of the net income and principal of the trust
as the Trustee, in the Trustee's absolute discretion, shall determine to be advisable, giving
primary consideration to the Grantor's lifetime needs and comfort. In this regard, any concern
for preserving a fund to be turned over upon the Grantor's death shall be entirely subordinate to
providing for the Grantor in a liberal and generous manner. The Trustee shall accumulate and
add to principal any net income not so paid or applied.
CLG-Sub 2_00171

2. Disposition After Grantor's Death. Upon the Grantor's death, the Trustee
shall distribute the remaining trust property, together with any property distributed to the Trustee
as a result of the Grantor's death, as provided in the following sections of this Agreement.
During the period of administration of the Grantor's estate and the post mortem administration of
this Trust, the Trustee shall determine, in the Trustee's absolute discretion, the appropriate time
or times for the distribution of trust property and the income therefrom to any beneficiary
hereinafter named.
3.
Distributions for Taxes and Expenses. Upon the Grantor's death, the
Trustee may pay or make arrangements for the payment of (i) the Grantor's secured and
unsecured debts; (ii) the Grantor's funeral and interment or cremation expenses, without regard
to any statutory limits; (iii) the administration expenses of the Grantor's estate; and (iv) any
estate, inheritance, and other transfer taxes, by whatever name called, including all interest and
penalties thereon, that are due by reason of the Grantor's death ("estate taxes") and are
attributable to any property passing hereunder or any retirement plan account which does not
pass hereunder but is payable to beneficiaries named hereunder (together, "estate taxes and
expenses").
All estate taxes and expenses paid by the Trustee shall be paid out of the
Trust Residue passing under section 5. Estate taxes and expenses that are attributable to any
other property shall be apportioned to and paid by the recipients of such property, except that in
making the apportionment, allowances shall be made for any exemptions granted and for any
deductions and credits allowed by the law imposing the tax.
The Trustee may pay estate taxes and expenses without the necessity of
any court order. In the payment of estate taxes and expenses, the Trustee may rely upon the
2
CLG-Sub 2_00172

certification of the Grantor's Personal Representative to the effect that any such estate taxes and
expenses are payable.
4.
Disposition of Grantor's Residence; Disposition of Tangible Personal
Property.
4.1
Disposition of
4.1(1)
Grantor's Residence. Upon the Grantor's death, if
JANE survives the Grantor, JANE shall have the exclusive right to occupy the real property
situated at 5636 Western Avenue, Chevy Chase Maryland (the "Grantor's Residence") for the
period necessary for JANE to relocate to a new residence and to arrange for the storage, sale, or
transfer of her tangible personal property located at the Grantor's death in the Grantor's
Residence. During such period, JANE may reside in the Grantor's Residence and/or keep her
tangible personal property in the Grantor's Residence free of any obligation to pay rent and free
of any obligation to pay any expense of the Grantor's Residence. It is the Grantor's desire that

Trustee shall have full authority and discretion to accomplish the sale of the Grantor's Residence
upon the terms and conditions and within such timeframes as the Trustee, in the sole and

beneficiaries thereof. Any and all expenses of maintaining the Grantor's Residence following the
Grantor's death and all costs related to its sale shall be paid by the Trustee as expenses of

6.2
Incapacitated Trustees. In the event a Trustee shall become
incapacitated, he or she shall cease to serve as Trustee during such period of incapacity. For
purposes of this Agreement, the term "incapacitated" shall mean any one or more of the
following: (i) appointment by a court of competent jurisdiction of a guardian of the person
and/or property of the Trustee; (ii) certification by two (2) licensed physicians who have
personally examined the Trustee that the Trustee is substantially incapable of managing his or
her financial affairs; or (iii) certification in writing by the Trustee's spouse that in the opinion of
such spouse the Trustee is substantially incapable of managing his or her financial affairs. Any
person who shall make a certification in accordance with the foregoing may subsequently certify
that the Trustee is no longer incapacitated. Upon the effective date of any certification that the
Trustee is no longer incapacitated, the Trustee may resume service as a Trustee hereunder. Any
determination that a Trustee is incapacitated shall be binding unless a court of competent
jurisdiction makes a contrary determination.

any form of insurance coverage, not otherwise required by Lender, for damage to, or destruction
of, the Property, such policy shall include a standard mortgage clause and shall name Lender as
mortgagee and/or as an additional loss payee.
In the event of loss, Borrower shall give prompt notice to the insurance carrier and
Lender. Lender may make proof of loss if not made promptly by Borrower. Unless Lender and
Borrower otherwise agree in writing, any insurance proceeds, whether or not the underlying
insurance was required by Lender, shall be applied to restoration or repair of the Property, if the
restoration or repair is economically feasible and Lender's security is not lessened. If the
restoration or repair is not economically feasible or Lender's security would be lessened, the
insurance proceeds shall be applied to the sums secured by this Security Instrument, whether or
not then due, with the excess, if any, paid to Borrower. Such insurance proceeds shall be applied
in the order provided for in Section 2.
If Borrower abandons the Property, Lender may file, negotiate and settle any available
insurance claim and related matters. If Borrower does not respond within 30 days to a notice
from Lender that the insurance carrier has offered to settle a claim, then Lender may negotiate
and settle the claim. The 30-day period will begin when the notice is given. In either event, or if
Lender acquires the Property under Section 22 or otherwise, Borrower hereby assigns to Lender
(a) Borrower's rights to any insurance proceeds in an amount not to exceed the amounts unpaid
under the Note or this Security Instrument, and (b) any other of Borrower's rights (other than the
right to any refund of unearned premiums paid by Borrower) under all insurance policies
covering the Property, insofar as such rights are applicable to the coverage of the Property.
Lender may use the insurance proceeds either to repair or restore the Property or to pay amounts
unpaid under the Note or this Security Instrument, whether or not then due.

11.
Assignment of Miscellaneous Proceeds; Forfeiture.
All Miscellaneous
Proceeds are hereby assigned to and shall be paid to Lender.
If the Property is damaged, such Miscellaneous Proceeds shall be applied to restoration or
repair of the Property, if the restoration or repair is economically feasible and Lender's security is
not lessened. During such repair and restoration period, Lender shall have the right to hold such
Miscellaneous Proceeds until Lender has had an opportunity to inspect such Property to ensure
the work has been completed to Lender's satisfaction, provided that such inspection shall be
undertaken promptly. Lender may pay for the repairs and restoration in a single disbursement or
in a series of progress payments as the work is completed. Unless an agreement is made in
writing or Applicable Law requires interest to be paid on such Miscellaneous Proceeds, Lender
shall not be required to pay Borrower any interest or earnings on such Miscellaneous Proceeds. If
the restoration or repair is not economically feasible or Lender's security would be lessened, the
Miscellaneous Proceeds shall be applied to the sums secured by this Security Instrument, whether
or not then due, with the excess, if any, paid to Borrower. Such Miscellaneous Proceeds shall be
applied in the order provided for in Section 2.
In the event of a total taking, destruction, or loss in value of the Property, the
Miscellaneous Proceeds shall be applied to the sums secured by this Security Instrument, whether
or not then due, with the excess, if any, paid to Borrower.
In the event of a partial taking, destruction, or loss in value of the Property in which the
fair market value of the Property immediately before the partial taking, destruction, or loss in
value is equal to or greater than the amount of the sums secured by this Security Instrument
immediately before the partial taking, destruction, or loss in value, unless Borrower and Lender
otherwise agree in writing, the sums secured by this Security Instrument shall be reduced by the

waiver of or preclude the exercise of any right or remedy.

21.
Hazardous Substances. As used in this Section 21: (a) "Hazardous Substances"
are those substances defined as toxic or hazardous substances, pollutants, or wastes by
Environmental Law and the following substances: gasoline, kerosene, other flammable or toxic
petroleum products, toxic pesticides and herbicides, volatile solvents, materials containing
asbestos or formaldehyde, and radioactive materials; (b) "Environmental Law" means federal
laws and laws of the jurisdiction where the Property is located that relate to health, safety or
environmental protection; (c) "Environmental Cleanup" includes any response action, remedial
action, or removal action, as defined in Environmental Law; and (d) an "Environmental
Condition" means a condition that can cause, contribute to, or otherwise trigger an
Environmental Cleanup.
Borrower shall not cause or permit the presence, use, disposal, storage, or release of any
Hazardous Substances, or threaten to release any Hazardous Substances, on or in the Property.
Borrower shall not do, nor allow anyone else to do, anything affecting the Property (a) that is in
violation of any Environmental Law, (b) which creates an Environmental Condition, or (c)
which, due to the presence, use, or release of a Hazardous Substance, creates a condition that
adversely affects the value of the Property. The preceding two sentences shall not apply to the
presence, use, or storage on the Property of small quantities of Hazardous Substances that are
generally recognized to be appropriate to normal residential uses and to maintenance of the
Property (including, but not limited to, hazardous substances in consumer products).
Borrower shall promptly give Lender written notice of (a) any investigation, claim,

demand, lawsuit or other action by any governmental or regulatory agency or private party
involving the Property and any Hazardous Substance or Environmental Law of which Borrower
has actual knowledge, (b) any Environmental Condition, including but not limited to, any

condition caused by the presence, use or release of a Hazardous Substance which adversely
affects the value of the Property. If Borrower learns, or is notified by any governmental or

22.
Acceleration; Remedies. Lender shall give notice to Borrower prior to
acceleration following Borrower's breach of any covenant or agreement in this Security
Instrument (but not prior to acceleration under Section 18 unless Applicable Law provides
otherwise). The notice shall specify: (a) the default; (b) the action required to cure the
default; (c) a date, not less than 30 days from the date the notice is given to Borrower, by
which the default must be cured; and (d) that failure to cure the default on or before the
date specified in the notice may result in acceleration of the sums secured by this Security
Instrument and sale of the Property. The notice shall further inform Borrower of the right
to reinstate after acceleration and the right to assert in the foreclosure proceeding the non-
existence of a default or any other defense of Borrower to acceleration and sale. If the
default is not cured on or before the date specified in the notice, Lender at its option may
require immediate payment in full of all sums secured by this Security Instrument without
further demand and may invoke the power of sale, assent to decree, and/or any other
remedies permitted by Applicable Law. Lender shall be entitled to collect all expenses
incurred in pursuing the remedies provided in this Section 22, including, but not limited to,
reasonable attorneys' fees and costs of title evidence.
If Lender invokes the power of sale, Lender shall mail or cause Trustee to mail a
notice of sale to Borrower in the manner prescribed by Applicable Law. Trustee shall give
notice of sale by public advertisement and by such other means as required by Applicable
Law. Trustee, without demand on Borrower, shall sell the Property at public auction to the
highest bidder at the time and place and under the terms designated in the notice of sale in
one or more parcels and in any order Trustee determines. Trustee may postpone sale of all
or any parcel of the Property by public announcement at the time and place of any
previously scheduled sale and by notice to any other persons as required by Applicable
Law. Lender or its designee may purchase the Property at any sale.
Trustee shall deliver to the purchaser Trustee's deed conveying the Property
without any covenant or warranty, expressed or implied. The recitals in the Trustee's deed
shall be prima facie evidence of the truth of the statements made therein. Trustee shall
apply the proceeds of the sale in the following order: (a) to all expenses of the sale,
including, but not limited to, Trustee's fees of 2.5% of the gross sale price and reasonable
attorneys' fees; (b) to all sums secured by this Security Instrument; and (c) any excess to
the person or persons legally entitled to it.
